questions.prompt: What finally makes a very massive star explode?
options: It runs out of fuel layer by layer, and its iron core can no longer release energy, so it collapses in about a second
Another star hits it
It gets too hot for its own skin and pops
A comet smacks into it
questions.explanation: Fusion builds layers up to iron at the center. Iron takes energy to fuse rather than giving it, so the core suddenly has no energy source — gravity collapses it in about a second.
questions.misconception: Explosions read as 'too much fuel catching fire' — but the fuse is the opposite: fuel that can no longer burn is what lets gravity win the round.

questions.prompt: What physically tears the star apart?
options: The heat of the core melts the gas
A shock wave rebounds off the collapsed core and blasts through the infalling envelope
The star's own rotation shreds it
Space rocks strike from outside
questions.explanation: The collapsing core stops suddenly at neutron density and bounces back like a spring; that bounce sends a shock wave racing outward at close to light speed, blowing the envelope into space.
questions.misconception: The explosion reads as 'something in the middle blows up' — but the tearing comes from the rebound, the same way a bouncing ball throws a wave outward.

questions.prompt: Where did Earth's gold and uranium come from?
options: They were always here, from the Big Bang onward
They were forged in supernovae that exploded before the solar system existed
They came from deep under Earth's crust, made by pressure alone
Comets imported them from another galaxy
questions.explanation: Big-bang nucleosynthesis only made the lightest elements. Everything heavier than iron — gold, silver, uranium — is forged in supernovae, so the atoms in Earth and in you predate the Sun.
questions.misconception: 'Earth is old' makes it seem enough, but the Earth is much younger than its own matter; the heavy atoms carried into it were minted in stellar explosions billions of years earlier.

questions.prompt: How bright does a supernova get compared with the rest of its galaxy?
options: About as bright as one star
Brighter than its whole galaxy for a few weeks — tens of billions of stars worth of light
Brighter than the Sun but dimmer than the galaxy
It is invisible except to special telescopes
questions.explanation: For a few weeks, a single supernova outshines the combined light of all the billions of ordinary stars in its home galaxy — one of the brightest events in space.
questions.misconception: Comparisons with the Sun cap the imagination; 'as bright as a galaxy for weeks' stretches it correctly — that is why supernovae of other galaxies are discovered from Earth to this day.

questions.prompt: What is left at the center after a core-collapse supernova?
options: Nothing at all — the star vanishes without a trace
Either a neutron star or a black hole, depending on how massive the core is
A fresh main-sequence star
A fleet of new planets
questions.explanation: The collapsed core survives as a neutron star (up to ~2-3 solar masses) or, for the very heaviest cores, keeps collapsing into a black hole.
questions.misconception: After such a violent event, 'completely gone' feels natural — but the densest residue always remains, and what it becomes is decided by the core's mass on the way down.
